cues.text: A Substitute Missionary

Born Jozef De Veuster in 1840 to a farming family in Tremelo, Belgium, the future saint entered the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary at nineteen, taking the religious name Damien after a fourth-century physician-martyr.
When his own brother, a member of the same congregation, fell ill and could not travel to a mission assignment in Hawaii, Damien volunteered to take his place.
He arrived in Honolulu in March 1864 and was ordained a priest there two months later.
A Colony of Exile
In 1865, alarmed by the spread of leprosy (Hansen's disease), the Hawaiian government authorized an isolation settlement on the Kalaupapa Peninsula; the first patients arrived there in 1866.
Located on the island of Molokai, it forcibly deported those diagnosed with the disease, with little regard for their welfare once quarantined.
By 1873, conditions in the colony had deteriorated badly, medical care was minimal, and its residents, desperate for spiritual and pastoral care, begged for a resident priest.
Choosing to Stay
Damien volunteered for what was initially meant to be a rotating three-month chaplaincy at the colony, arriving in May 1873.
Upon witnessing the residents' suffering and isolation firsthand, he asked to remain permanently rather than return after his assigned term.
He wrote candidly of the physical horror of his early visits and the 'fetid' odor of advanced disease.
At times, it forced him to step outside for fresh air.
He admitted taking up pipe-smoking partly to mask the smell that clung to his clothing.
Priest, Builder, and Advocate
Damien became far more than a chaplain to the colony: he built houses, churches, and roads with his own hands.
He organized medical care as best he could with the limited means available and tirelessly petitioned Hawaiian government officials to honor promises of support for the settlement.
This advocacy frequently strained his relationships with both civil authorities and his own religious superiors, who worried about the dangers and demands of his increasingly solitary mission.
Contracting the Disease
After more than a decade of intimate daily contact with those suffering from leprosy, Damien himself contracted the disease in 1884.
He accepted the diagnosis without surprise or complaint, continuing his ministry among his parishioners even as his own health steadily declined.
He died at Kalaupapa on 15 April 1889, sixteen years after first volunteering for what he had assumed would be a brief assignment.
Legacy

Damien's body was returned to Belgium in 1936, though a relic of his hand was later sent back to be reburied at his original Molokai grave in 1995, the same year he was beatified by Pope John Paul II .
Canonized in 2009 by Pope Benedict XVI, Damien remains one of the most widely admired missionary saints of the modern era.
He is honored as patron of those with leprosy, HIV and AIDS, and all who suffer incurable illness—a priest who chose permanent exile among the outcast rather than a brief, safe visit.
